The instance-level QE signal averages over all pairs:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sj_instance}
c_{\text{sj}}(x) = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}} \sum_{i<j} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)
\end{equation}
For selection, $c_{\text{sj}}(x)$ cannot rank individual candidates (it assigns one score per input).
Consensus-proximity converts it to a per-sample utility $u_{\text{sj}}(y_i) = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, selecting the candidate most consistent with the sample pool---equivalent to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling} with SJ as the utility function.
The same construction applies to FK, EM, and VC.

\item \textbf{Diagnosis of the correlation-selection gap.}
    The gap operates at two layers.
    \textit{Definitional}: four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates; consensus-proximity (MBR) conversion yields per-sample rankings but does not recover selection ability.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).
